maml:description.maml:para: Reads a text file, detecting its character encoding.
Reads a text file and writes its content to the pipeline as strings, one object per line.

When -Encoding is omitted the character encoding of the file is detected. A byte order mark at the start of the file is always skipped, so U+FEFF never leaks into the first line. Only that first byte order mark is removed; a second U+FEFF that follows it is kept as a character. If the file ends in the middle of a character (for example, a UTF-16 file of odd length), the incomplete bytes are read as a replacement character, as in PowerShell 7.x.
Unlike the built-in Get-Content, the same name passed to -Encoding produces the same result on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x.
Path to the target file. Wildcards are permitted.

Character encoding used to decode the file. When omitted (or set to Auto) the file is detected. When specified, no detection is performed, which is the way to override a misdetection. A byte order mark at the start of the file is always skipped, whatever is specified here. Unified vocabulary: Auto, utf8NoBOM, utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, unicodeBOM, bigendianunicodeNoBOM, bigendianunicodeBOM, utf32NoBOM, utf32BOM, bigendianutf32NoBOM, bigendianutf32BOM, ascii, ansi, oem, utf7 (reading only). Any WebName known to .NET (shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, big5, gb18030, ...), any numeric code page (932, 65001, ...), a System.Text.Encoding instance, and an EncodingInformation object returned by Resolve-Encoding are also accepted. Only that first byte order mark is removed; a second U+FEFF that follows it is kept as a character. If the file ends in the middle of a character (for example, a UTF-16 file of odd length), the incomplete bytes are read as a replacement character, as in PowerShell 7.x. A detection result that has gone through Export-Clixml and Import-Clixml, a job, remoting or Select-Object is no longer an EncodingInformation object and is not accepted; pass its CodePage, or a unified vocabulary name that states the BOM (such as unicodeBOM), instead.

Returns the entire file as a single string instead of splitting it into lines. This is the only lossless way to read a file: splitting into lines discards whether each line ended with CR-LF or LF, and whether the file ended with a line break at all. Cannot be combined with -TotalCount. For an empty file (0 bytes, or only a BOM), -Raw returns an empty string, whereas the built-in Get-Content -Raw returns nothing ($null).

Reads only the first N lines of each file. Cannot be combined with -Raw. The aliases -Head and -First can also be used, as with Get-Content. When omitted, all lines are read. Negative values, including -1, are not accepted (as with Get-Content in PowerShell 7.x; Get-Content in Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads all lines for -1); to read all lines, omit -TotalCount.

Culture name used when detecting the character encoding, such as ko-KR. Combinations that the bytes alone cannot tell apart - EUC-KR and CP949, or EUC-JP and Shift_JIS - are resolved with the culture, so specify the culture of the target language when reading Korean or Chinese files on a Japanese system. maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.
Detection reads the whole file. A source file whose first megabyte is pure ASCII and which contains Japanese comments only near the end is therefore detected correctly.
Detection failure and a missing file are reported as non-terminating errors, as with the built-in Get-Content. Use -ErrorAction Stop to turn them into terminating errors.
Reading and writing the same file in one pipeline is rejected, because the downstream command would truncate the file before it has been read. Receive the content into a variable first.

Single-byte character encodings (windows-1252, ISO-8859-x, ...) cannot be distinguished by their byte structure and are estimated from text statistics. Whether detection succeeds therefore depends more on the content than on the length: text containing a list of characters, lines full of symbols and digits, or characters rarely used in the language may not be detected (CodePage -1) even when it is several hundred bytes long. In that case, specify the code page with -Encoding.

A main-stream name such as a.txt::$DATA is treated as the same file as a.txt. Alternate data streams (such as a.txt:alt) are not read or written; they cause the error AlternateDataStreamNotSupported (the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x).

maml:description.maml:para: Writes a text file with the character encoding, BOM and line break stated explicitly.
Writes content to a file, replacing anything the file contained.

The same name passed to -Encoding produces the same bytes on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. In particular, 'utf8NoBOM' writes UTF-8 without a BOM on both, which the built-in Set-Content cannot do on PowerShell 5.1.

When -Encoding is omitted, the character encoding, the BOM and the line break are inherited from the file being overwritten, so overwriting does not silently change the nature of an existing file. To inherit from the file the content was read from instead, use -EncodingFrom.

Path to the target file. Wildcards are permitted. The file is created if it does not exist, unless the character encoding has to be inherited from it (see -Encoding). If the wildcard matches no file, nothing is written and the non-terminating error ItemNotFound is reported (the same as Set-Content / Add-Content). To create a file whose name contains wildcard characters, use -LiteralPath.

Content to write. Each element is written followed by a line break, including the last one, unless -NoNewline is specified. Values that are not strings are converted with the PowerShell type converter, which uses the invariant culture. $null elements of an array are skipped (as with Set-Content and Add-Content). Dates and numbers therefore do not follow the current culture, unlike Set-Content and Add-Content (a date is written as 10/15/2026 14:30:00 and 1.5 as 1.5 in any culture). Some numbers are still formatted differently by the .NET of each host: -0.0 is written as -0 on PowerShell 7.x and as 0 on Windows PowerShell 5.1.

Character encoding, and BOM policy, used to write the file. When omitted (or set to Auto) they are inherited from the existing file at the destination; if that file does not exist the command reports an error. Cannot be combined with -EncodingFrom. Unified vocabulary: Auto, utf8NoBOM, utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, unicodeBOM, bigendianunicodeNoBOM, bigendianunicodeBOM, utf32NoBOM, utf32BOM, bigendianutf32NoBOM, bigendianutf32BOM, ascii, ansi, oem, utf7 (reading only). Any WebName known to .NET (shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, big5, gb18030, ...), any numeric code page (932, 65001, ...), a System.Text.Encoding instance, and an EncodingInformation object returned by Resolve-Encoding are also accepted. A detection result that has gone through Export-Clixml and Import-Clixml, a job, remoting or Select-Object is no longer an EncodingInformation object and is not accepted; pass its CodePage, or a unified vocabulary name that states the BOM (such as unicodeBOM), instead.

Inherits the character encoding, the BOM policy and the line break from the given reference file. The value is used exactly as typed; wildcards are not expanded. An explicit -LineBreak still wins over the inherited line break. Cannot be combined with -Encoding.

Does not write a line break between elements or at the end. Required for a lossless round trip of content read with Get-ProbedContent -Raw. When -LineBreak is also specified a warning is issued, because the line break simply goes unused.

Line break to write: Auto, CrLf, Lf or Cr. Auto inherits the line break from the reference information if there is any (-EncodingFrom, -Encoding Auto, or an EncodingInformation passed to -Encoding), and otherwise uses the operating system default. When the reference file has mixed line breaks, CR-LF is inherited if the file contains any CR-LF and LF otherwise; this rule does not depend on the operating system. Only the line break written after each element is decided; line breaks contained in a value (for example "a`nb") are written as they are. To unify the line breaks in a file, use Convert-ProbedContent.

Writes to a file that has the read-only attribute set, by clearing the attribute temporarily; the attribute is restored after writing, even if writing fails. This switch has no effect on anything else.
Shows what would happen if the cmdlet runs. The file is not modified. Checks that do not modify files (such as a read-only file) are still performed, and their errors are reported.
Prompts for confirmation before running the cmdlet.

If restoring also fails, the copy is kept in the temporary folder and the error message shows its path. With this method, a file of 1 MiB or smaller can be left partly written if the process is forcibly terminated while writing (for example, by a power failure). Symbolic links and junctions are followed to the end, and the target of the link is written (the link itself remains). For a file larger than 1 MiB that is a hard link (two or more links) or is in a folder in which files cannot be created, the original file is first copied to the temporary folder and then written directly; if writing fails, it is restored from the copy. Copying takes time for a large file. With every method, the attributes (read-only, hidden), the creation time, alternate data streams and the ACL are kept. On both hosts, a wildcard that matches several files reads them all, and a missing file or duplicate column names are non-terminating errors, so the remaining files are still read.
-Culture and -UseCulture are different: -Culture is the culture used to detect the character encoding, and -UseCulture is a switch that makes the delimiter the list separator of the current culture.
-DetectionLineCount counts physical lines, not CSV records. When it is specified the whole file is verified, so each file is read twice. Specifying -Encoding skips both detection and verification.

Single-byte character encodings (windows-1252, ISO-8859-x, ...) cannot be distinguished by their byte structure and are estimated from text statistics. Whether detection succeeds therefore depends more on the content than on the length: text containing a list of characters, lines full of symbols and digits, or characters rarely used in the language may not be detected (CodePage -1) even when it is several hundred bytes long. In that case, specify the code page with -Encoding.
The verification done for -DetectionLineCount cannot always find a misdetected single-byte character encoding, because almost any byte sequence decodes to valid characters in a single-byte encoding.

maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.

All failures of this cmdlet are terminating errors, because there is always exactly one output file. Checks that do not modify files (a read-only file, -NoClobber, and the detection and verification of existing files) are performed before -WhatIf and -Confirm take effect, so their errors are reported with -WhatIf as well.

The CSV rules follow PowerShell 7.x on both hosts. Differences from the built-in Export-Csv: the default character encoding is utf8NoBOM on Windows PowerShell 5.1 as well (the built-in cmdlet of 5.1 writes ASCII, so Japanese becomes ???); no #TYPE line is written by default; -UseQuotes, -QuoteFields and -NoHeader are available on 5.1; and dictionaries are written with their keys as columns. -Append inherits the character encoding and the line break of the existing file and checks consistency, and when the last line of the existing file has no line break, one is added before the first record (the built-in cmdlet joins the lines). Reading and writing the same file in one pipeline (Import-ProbedCsv a.csv | Export-ProbedCsv a.csv) stops with SamePathRoundTrip instead of emptying the file.

Omitting -Encoding and specifying Auto mean different things. Omitted: utf8NoBOM for a new or overwritten file, and inherited from the target for -Append. Auto: inherited from the existing output file, which must exist. This differs from Set-ProbedContent, where omitting -Encoding means Auto.

With -Append, the records are written in the column order and spelling of the header of the existing file (column names are matched without regard to case), and the header and #TYPE lines are not written. A file that contains only a BOM is given a header. The file appended to is always detected (and, with -DetectionLineCount, verified), because its header and its last line break have to be read.

The columns are decided by the first object. Properties of later objects, and of appended objects, that are not among the columns are silently not written, as with the built-in Export-Csv. Missing properties are written as empty values.
-LineBreak decides only the line break written after each record and after the header. Line breaks inside values are written as they are.
For a CSV file to be opened in Excel, use utf8BOM or shift_jis: Excel may misread UTF-8 without a BOM.
-Culture and -UseCulture are different: -Culture is the culture used to detect the character encoding, and -UseCulture is a switch that makes the delimiter the list separator of the current culture.

-DetectionLineCount counts physical lines, not CSV records. When it is specified, an existing file is verified as a whole before anything is written, so that file is read twice. Specifying -Encoding skips the detection and verification of the output file, but with -Append the file appended to is still detected.

A BOM is written only when at least one line is written. When no input arrives, the output file is created empty (or truncated to 0 bytes) without a BOM; with -Append an existing file is left untouched.

Single-byte character encodings (windows-1252, ISO-8859-x, ...) cannot be distinguished by their byte structure and are estimated from text statistics. Whether detection succeeds therefore depends more on the content than on the length: text containing a list of characters, lines full of symbols and digits, or characters rarely used in the language may not be detected (CodePage -1) even when it is several hundred bytes long. In that case, specify the code page with -Encoding instead of using Auto or inheriting it with -Append.
The verification done for -DetectionLineCount cannot always find a misdetected single-byte character encoding, because almost any byte sequence decodes to valid characters in a single-byte encoding.

If the text contains a character that cannot be represented in the character encoding of the destination, nothing is written to the file: the cmdlet reports the terminating error UnrepresentableCharacter (the same ID as Convert-ProbedContent). The message shows the code point (U+XXXX) of the first such character and the name of the character encoding. Characters are never replaced with '?' or a similar character (such as é with e). Lines already written are also discarded, and the file is restored to its state before the command (an overwrite restores the original content; an append is truncated back to the original length). When a System.Text.Encoding instance is passed to -Encoding, its fallback settings are not used.

When the inherited character encoding (from the destination or the file being appended to, the -EncodingFrom reference, or an EncodingInformation passed to -Encoding) is us-ascii, the text is written as UTF-8 without a BOM. A file whose bytes are all below 0x80 is also valid UTF-8, so you can add non-ASCII text to a log or CSV that contains only ASCII characters. When only ASCII characters are written, the bytes are the same as us-ascii. An explicit -Encoding ascii stays us-ascii. The append consistency check also treats a us-ascii file being appended to as UTF-8 without a BOM.

An overwrite is written to a temporary file in the same folder as the target (.~probed<8 hex digits>.probedtmp), which replaces the target only when writing is complete, so the original file is unchanged if writing fails midway. However, when both the content and the original file are 1 MiB or smaller, no temporary file is used: the content of the original file is copied into memory, the original file is written directly, and if writing fails it is restored from the copy in memory (a file that does not exist yet is created and written directly, and deleted if writing fails). If restoring also fails, the copy is kept in the temporary folder and the error message shows its path. With this method, a file of 1 MiB or smaller can be left partly written if the process is forcibly terminated while writing (for example, by a power failure). Symbolic links and junctions are followed to the end, and the target of the link is written (the link itself remains). For a file larger than 1 MiB that is a hard link (two or more links) or is in a folder in which files cannot be created, the original file is first copied to the temporary folder and then written directly; if writing fails, it is restored from the copy. Copying takes time for a large file. With every method, the attributes (read-only, hidden), the creation time, alternate data streams and the ACL are kept. On Linux / macOS the permissions of the original file are carried over, but the owner is not, and hard links to a file larger than 1 MiB are broken. The name of the temporary file does not contain the name of the target (to stay within the length limits of names and paths), so if the process is terminated during writing, a temporary file left behind cannot be traced back to its target by its name; it is in the same folder as the target. If the path of the temporary file would exceed the length limit, the original file is copied to the temporary folder and written directly instead. A file that has been written gets the Archive attribute, as with Set-Content; when writing is undone, the attributes are left as they were.

Appending writes directly to the existing file. Symbolic links are followed and the target is appended to; when the target of a link does not exist, a file is created there, as Add-Content / Out-File -Append do. When the command stops with an error (an unrepresentable character, the consistency check EncodingChangeOnAppend, or a write failure), everything written to the file by that call is removed and the file returns to its length before the append (a file created by the append is deleted).

When another process has the target open, an overwrite fails not when the file is opened but when writing is completed (WriteFailed and so on). The original file is still unchanged, and no temporary file is left. Replacing a file larger than 1 MiB fails if the other process does not allow sharing for delete; writing directly to a file of 1 MiB or smaller fails if it does not allow sharing for write.
When the destination is a symbolic link whose target does not exist, the file is created at the target of the link, as Out-File / Export-Csv do (the link itself remains).

Whether two paths are the same file (writing to a file that is being read, SamePathRoundTrip; a -Destination of Convert-ProbedContent that is the source itself) is decided by the file itself, not by the path string. \\?\, administrative UNC shares (\\localhost\C$\...), \\.\, subst drives, symbolic links, junctions, hard links and differences in case are all recognized as the same file. On Linux / macOS paths are compared after resolving links, so hard links are regarded as different files.

A main-stream name such as a.txt::$DATA is treated as the same file as a.txt. Alternate data streams (such as a.txt:alt) are not read or written; they cause the error AlternateDataStreamNotSupported (the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x).

Resolves the many forms this module accepts for a character encoding into a single System.Text.Encoding instance.

This is a specialised command, meant for calling .NET class library APIs (System.IO.StreamReader, System.IO.File, XmlWriter and so on) directly from PowerShell. If you only want to read or write files, use Get-ProbedContent, Set-ProbedContent or Add-ProbedContent instead; they take exactly the same values for -Encoding and you do not have to convert anything yourself.

Any WebName known to .NET (shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, big5, gb18030, ...), any numeric code page (932, 65001, ...), a System.Text.Encoding instance, and an EncodingInformation object returned by Resolve-Encoding are also accepted. Auto is not accepted. A detection result that has gone through Export-Clixml and Import-Clixml, a job, remoting or Select-Object is no longer an EncodingInformation object and is not accepted; pass its CodePage, or a unified vocabulary name that states the BOM (such as unicodeBOM), instead.

maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.

When a System.Text.Encoding instance is passed directly, its own GetPreamble() decides whether a BOM is written. [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8 and [System.Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(65001) both return BOM-emitting instances, so passing them writes a BOM. Use (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false) for UTF-8 without a BOM, or simply use the vocabulary names, which state the BOM policy explicitly.

UTF-16 and UTF-32 without a BOM ('unicodeNoBOM', 'bigendianunicodeNoBOM', 'utf32NoBOM', 'bigendianutf32NoBOM') are supported so that every state the detector can report can also be written back, but they are NOT recommended: without a BOM there is no reliable way for another program to tell the byte order, or to tell the file apart from a single-byte encoding.

The BOM policy of the returned instance follows the name: 'utf8BOM' returns an instance that emits a BOM and 'utf8NoBOM' one that does not. For a bare 'utf8' the instance does not emit a BOM, which is why the writing cmdlets refuse that name instead of guessing.

UTF-7 is obsolete and .NET 5 and later refuse to create it through Encoding.GetEncoding. This cmdlet constructs it directly, so 'utf7' works on both PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x. It is supported for reading legacy data only.

maml:description.maml:para: Detects the character encoding of a text file.

Detects the character encoding of a file and returns an EncodingInformation object describing it: the code page, the WebName, whether the file has a byte order mark, the line break in use, and the culture the detector assumed.
The object can be passed straight to -Encoding of Get-ProbedContent, Set-ProbedContent and Add-ProbedContent, and to ConvertTo-DotNetEncoding.
Path to the file to detect.

Culture name used to resolve ambiguities that the bytes alone cannot settle, such as EUC-JP versus Shift_JIS. Defaults to the culture of the current session. Whether a name is accepted is decided by its form (BCP 47), the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. Names such as C, root and POSIX are not accepted and cause the terminating error InvalidCulture. A well-formed name that does not exist (such as xx-YY) is accepted, but it matches none of the East Asian language areas. An extended language subtag right after the language (yue in zh-yue) is used as the language, as RFC 5646 defines, so zh-yue is treated as Cantonese (Traditional Chinese, Hong Kong). Spaces and tabs before and after the name are ignored, as with -Encoding and -Strategy (' ko-KR' is the same as 'ko-KR'); a space inside the name is not accepted.

Detection strategy: Combined (default), NativeOnly or UtfUnknownOnly. Combined runs the built-in detector first and falls back to UTF.Unknown only when it cannot decide. A value that cannot be interpreted causes the terminating error InvalidStrategy, the same as the other commands. HZ-GB-2312 and UTF-7, whose bytes are all below 0x80, are not detected by Combined or NativeOnly: they are reported as us-ascii and their escape sequences are read as they are. UtfUnknownOnly detects HZ-GB-2312. To read these files reliably, specify the character encoding explicitly (for example -Encoding 52936 or -Encoding utf7 in the commands that have -Encoding).

maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.

The PSEncodingName property means different things on the two hosts: on PowerShell 7.x it is a registered friendly name such as 'utf8BOM', while on Windows PowerShell 5.1 it is only filled in when the result happens to match one of the fixed -Encoding values of 5.1, and is otherwise null. UsePSName says whether the value can be passed to the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets. The unified vocabulary of Get-ProbedContent, Set-ProbedContent and Add-ProbedContent does not have this problem.

Single-byte character encodings (windows-1252, ISO-8859-x, ...) cannot be distinguished by their byte structure and are estimated from text statistics. Whether detection succeeds therefore depends more on the content than on the length: text containing a list of characters, lines full of symbols and digits, or characters rarely used in the language may not be detected (CodePage -1) even when it is several hundred bytes long. Resolve-Encoding has no way to specify the character encoding; specify -Encoding in the reading and writing cmdlets (-SourceEncoding for Convert-ProbedContent).

A UTF-16 or UTF-32 file without a BOM in which every byte is below 0x80 is detected as UTF-16 or UTF-32 only when every unit has the form of an alphanumeric character (for UTF-16LE, a byte other than 00 followed by 00); otherwise it is reported as us-ascii. Known limitations: (1) A file that also contains a character whose two bytes are both below 0x80, such as U+4E0A (0A 4E in UTF-16LE), U+5B57, U+3042 or U+3001, is reported as us-ascii. Import-ProbedCsv and Export-ProbedCsv read such a file correctly when -DetectionLineCount is specified. (2) A file of only a few bytes, such as 41 00, cannot be told apart from ASCII followed by 00; it is reported as UTF-16 or UTF-32 when it has that form. (3) A file that contains the character U+0000 is reported as us-ascii.

A main-stream name such as a.txt::$DATA is treated as the same file as a.txt. Alternate data streams (such as a.txt:alt) are not read or written; they cause the error AlternateDataStreamNotSupported (the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x). Errors: a file that does not exist, and a range larger than the limit with -DetectionLineCount, cause terminating errors (as before). A file that cannot be read (another program has it open without allowing others to read it, or access is denied), a file too large for whole-file detection (2 GB or larger) and insufficient memory cause non-terminating errors (ReadFailed, ReadAccessDenied, EncodingDetectionFailed, NotEnoughMemoryToDetect), and the next file is processed. A file that another program has open for writing can be read. Whole-file detection reads the file into memory and uses several times its size (about 3.6 times); on 32-bit Windows PowerShell 5.1, a file of several hundred MB can fail with NotEnoughMemoryToDetect. For large files, use -DetectionLineCount.
